findings.finding: Pass 1's audit ("grouping every inserted tag by FR + eyeballing file names against the FR's own spec title") validates at the file-name level, not the test level. Tagging a test as `@covers FR-X` asserts that test actually proves that FR's AC. A file-header mentioning FR-01.66 doesn't mean every test nested under the outermost describe proves FR-01.66 — unrelated helper tests in the same block will now be counted as covering that FR, which inflates coverage without changing real verification. This is materially different from deleting/weakening a test but violates the spirit of the AC ("no test is deleted or weakened to raise the number" — mis-tagging also raises the number dishonestly).
findings.suggestion: For every Pass 1 tag inserted above a block containing more than ~2–3 test cases, spot-check that the nested `it` titles actually exercise the FR. State in the ADR how many blocks were content-verified vs. name-verified, so the coverage delta is interpretable.

findings.finding: "Deduped to the outermost qualifying block so propagation covers everything nested under it" compounds the above: if a nested describe has no FR mention but sits under an outer block that does, it inherits the tag. Combined with the describe-scope stack, one broad header mention can bind a whole file of heterogeneous tests. The plan's own exclusion logic (near-miss catches in `triage-enrich` and `compliance-reader`) shows the heuristic is fragile — those two were caught by luck of phrasing.
findings.suggestion: Cap propagation: only tag blocks whose own text (describe title or local docstring) mentions the FR, falling back to header only when the entire file is single-concern (single top-level describe, or all describes plausibly under the FR). State the rule in the plan.

findings.finding: The `campaigns.events.test.ts` docstring "typo" correction (FR-01.31 → FR-01.33) is a judgment call embedded in an otherwise mechanical pass. If the original author meant FR-01.31 (e.g., the test did exercise network-profile behavior in a campaigns context), the "correction" rewrites intent based on file-name heuristics. The plan says the FR-01.31 test subject was "unrelated to the file's actual subject" but a GET endpoint test can legitimately cover network access profiling.
findings.suggestion: Record in the ADR the actual test titles under that header and why they can't plausibly relate to FR-01.31, so the correction is auditable.

findings.finding: The manifest is deliberately not committed (correct per `derived_snapshots.py` collision policy), but that means the headline 15.75% → 31.97% number is unverified against the CI gate's own run. If the scratch collector and CI collector ever diverge (different pinned revision, path resolution, working-tree differences), the merge-time regen could yield a different number — and the "no orphan/invalid tag regressions" claim goes untested until merge.
findings.suggestion: Confirm the scratch regen used the exact same pinned collector commit hash CI uses, and note the pin hash in the ADR. If CI's post-merge diff gates on `orphans`, verify the 12 pre-existing `FR-04.22` orphans are actually tolerated by the gate and not just "pre-existing."

findings.finding: Pass 2's FR-01.05 evidence cites a describe matching spec AC (F) "verbatim" — verbatim title matching is good evidence for that one describe, but FR-01.05 may have multiple ACs; tagging both files wholesale to FR-01.05 implies full-AC coverage. Same pattern for FR-01.16's "four describes are exactly that contract" (AC (E) is one of presumably several ACs).
findings.suggestion: When stating results, distinguish "FR has ≥1 bound test" (which is the actual metric — 32/32) from "FR is fully covered by its ACs." The plan reads correctly now, but ensure the ADR doesn't conflate them.

findings.finding: The automated rule can still over-tag mixed suites. Tagging the outermost qualifying `describe` deliberately propagates the FR to every nested test, even where a suite contains shared setup, regression cases, or a secondary concern that does not prove that FR. The stated filename/spec-title audit will not reliably detect this at test level.
findings.suggestion: Emit tags at the narrowest declaration that demonstrably exercises the FR. Require a per-inserted-target review list (file, suite/test title, resolved FR), especially for nested or multi-`describe` files; do not use outer-suite propagation where any descendant is unrelated.

findings.finding: The plan does not satisfy the explicit acceptance criterion to state derived and hand-mapped counts separately. It reports “21 FRs” from automation and five manual additions, but not the number of tagged tests/inserted bindings from each path. FR counts are not enough because each FR can cover many tests.
findings.suggestion: Include before/after totals plus separate counts for automated-derived bindings and manually verified bindings, ideally also the number of affected files and tests for each.

findings.finding: “Exactly one FR anywhere in the file” is only a weak proxy for semantic ownership. It misses aliasing through folded IDs, dynamically generated tests, parameterized tests, shared helpers, and ordinary prose that happens to name the sole FR; the cross-reference phrase list cannot make this generally safe.
findings.suggestion: Treat the script as candidate generation rather than an authority. Validate each candidate against the specific FR acceptance criterion and ensure the inserted comment binds the intended declaration under the collector’s actual parsing rules.

findings.finding: Incorrect tags on `FR-01.31` or the externally exposed org routes can falsely represent security-sensitive controls as tested. This is not a runtime vulnerability, but it weakens the integrity of compliance evidence precisely where reviewers may rely on it.
findings.suggestion: For the network-profile and host/secret-gate mappings, record the exact matching AC and test title in the review artifact, and confirm both positive and rejection/unauthorized paths are represented before attaching the security-related FR tag.

findings.finding: The reported “coverage” is traceability-tag coverage, not behavioral or product-test coverage. The large increase could be misunderstood as a substantial expansion in tested functionality.
findings.suggestion: Label all reported numbers as “bound-test traceability coverage” in the ADR/PR summary and retain the unchanged test pass counts alongside them.  The approach is directionally sound and appropriately avoids product changes, but it needs test-level attribution safeguards and the missing derived-versus-manual binding counts before it is ready. SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: revise
